title: Sharding / Partitioning
subtitle: Splitting the data across machines — and what you give up to do it
objectives: Explain when replication stops being enough and splitting is the only option left
Choose a shard key, and predict the hot shard it will create
Compare range and hash partitioning, and explain what consistent hashing solves
Account for what sharding costs: cross-shard queries, transactions, and resharding

exercises.prompt: Your database is drowning in WRITES. You add five read replicas. Does it help?
choices: Yes — five more machines share the work
No — every replica must apply every write, so you've added five machines that each do all the writing and none that do less
Yes, if you route writes to the replicas
exercises.why: Replication scales reads because any copy can answer a read, but every copy must perform every write — so a write bottleneck is untouched, and you've slightly worsened it by giving the leader five more followers to ship changes to. This is the asymmetry from unit 10 collecting its debt: copies cannot reduce write load, which leaves exactly one option — stop making every machine hold everything.

exercises.prompt: ______ splits your data across machines so each one holds only a subset of it.
exercises.why: Replication copies the whole dataset onto each machine; sharding divides it so each machine owns a slice. Copies versus slices — that one distinction is the whole difference between units 10 and 15.

exercises.prompt: Match each approach to what it does.

pairs.right: Every machine holds all the data
Each machine holds a slice of the data

exercises.why: They solve different problems and compose rather than compete: shard to divide the write load and the data, then replicate each shard so losing a machine doesn't lose that slice. Real systems at scale do both, because sharding alone gives you no redundancy — it just gives you more single points of failure.

exercises.prompt: Which problems does sharding actually solve? Select all.
choices: A dataset too large to fit on one machine
exercises.why: Splitting the data means each machine takes only its share of the writes, stores only its share of the bytes, AND answers only its share of the reads — so all three scale past one box. Survival is the one it doesn't buy: lose a shard and that slice is simply gone unless you also replicated it. Reads deserve a footnote though — sharding genuinely scales them, but it's rarely the right *tool* for them, because caching and read replicas buy the same relief without cross-shard queries, distributed transactions, or a shard key you can never change. The exception is when the working set outgrows one machine's memory, where replicas don't help (every copy has the same undersized cache) and only splitting the data does.

exercises.prompt: You shard users across 4 machines. Where does user 12345 live?
choices: On whichever machine is least busy
Wherever the shard key says — a rule maps that user's id to exactly one shard, and everyone applies the same rule
exercises.why: Sharding needs a deterministic rule mapping each row to one shard, because otherwise nobody could find it again — every reader and writer must independently compute the same answer. That rule's input is the shard key, and choosing it is the single most consequential decision in this unit: it decides where every row lives, forever, and it is brutally hard to change later.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'don't shard until you have to' such common advice?
choices: Because it permanently costs you cross-shard queries, cross-shard transactions, and painful resharding — costs you pay daily, for a scale you may not have
Because databases can't be sharded safely
exercises.why: Sharding is a one-way door that changes what your database can do: queries spanning shards get slow, transactions spanning shards get hard, and the shard key becomes an assumption baked into everything. Those bills arrive every day from the moment you shard, while the benefit only arrives when one machine genuinely can't cope — so the order matters enormously. Scale up, cache, and replicate first; shard when the ceiling is actually in sight.

exercises.prompt: You shard by user_id using ranges: users 1–1M on shard A, 1M–2M on B, and so on. Your ids auto-increment. What happens?
choices: Every new signup lands on the newest shard, so all your write traffic hammers one machine while the others idle
Old shards get all the writes
exercises.why: Sequential ids mean today's users all fall in the same range, so range-partitioning on them sends every insert to whichever shard owns the highest range — you built four machines and kept a one-machine write bottleneck. The general trap: range partitioning on any value that increases with time concentrates all new writes on one shard, which is exactly what you sharded to avoid.

exercises.prompt: Match each partitioning strategy to its behaviour.

pairs.right: Ordered slices — keeps range queries fast
Sequential keys create a hot shard
'All rows between X and Y' now hits every shard

exercises.why: It's the same tradeoff as B-trees versus hashing from unit 8, promoted to the level of machines: ordering buys you range scans and risks hotspots, while hashing buys you even distribution by deliberately destroying the order you'd need for ranges.

exercises.prompt: You hash user_id to pick a shard. What did that fix, and what did it break?
choices: Writes now spread evenly across shards — but 'give me all users created last week' must now ask every shard, because related rows are deliberately scattered
It fixed everything with no cost
It broke writes but fixed reads
exercises.why: Hashing spreads keys uniformly regardless of what the values mean, which is precisely why the hot shard disappears — and precisely why ordering does too. Rows that are adjacent in time or alphabet now sit on different machines by design, so any query defined by a range has to fan out to all of them and combine the results.

exercises.prompt: A chat app shards messages by hash(message_id). Loading one conversation is now slow. Why?
choices: The hash is slow to compute
A conversation's messages are scattered across every shard, so reading one chat means querying all of them
The shard key is too long
exercises.why: The shard key decided the physical layout, and hashing by message_id scattered messages that belong together — so the app's single most common query became a fan-out to every machine. Sharding by conversation_id instead would put a whole conversation on one shard and turn that query back into a single-shard read. The lesson: shard by whatever your hottest query filters on, so that query stays local.

exercises.prompt: So what's the rule for choosing a shard key?
choices: Pick something with many distinct values that spreads load evenly AND matches how you query, so your common reads stay on one shard
exercises.why: You're satisfying two demands at once: even distribution (or one machine becomes the bottleneck again) and query locality (or every read fans out). A random key nails the first and destroys the second; a sequential key does the reverse — the art is finding a key with high cardinality that also happens to be what your hot queries filter on.

exercises.prompt: You shard a multi-tenant SaaS app by tenant_id. What should worry you?
choices: Tenants aren't the same size: one enormous customer can outgrow a single shard, and no amount of rebalancing splits one tenant
exercises.why: Sharding by tenant gives beautiful query locality since almost every query is scoped to one tenant anyway — but it also means a tenant is indivisible, so your biggest customer must fit on one machine. That's usually a great trade right up until you land a whale, and then the fix is a composite key that can split a giant tenant further, which is much easier to design now than to retrofit.

exercises.prompt: You shard a social app by user_id. One user has 200 million followers. What breaks?
choices: Everything about that user lives on one shard, so that machine takes a wildly disproportionate share of traffic — a hot shard
exercises.why: Even a perfect hash spreads KEYS evenly, not LOAD — and load follows popularity, which is never uniform. This is the celebrity problem, and it's why real systems special-case their outliers: caching that user's data aggressively, or splitting their activity across a composite key. Any sharding scheme that assumes keys are equally busy will eventually meet a key that isn't.

exercises.prompt: You have 4 shards, assigned by hash(key) % 4. You add a fifth machine, making it % 5. What happens?
choices: Only the new shard's data moves
Almost every key now maps somewhere new, so the vast majority of your data has to move at once
exercises.why: Changing the modulus changes the answer for nearly every key, so adding one machine triggers a near-total reshuffle of the dataset — while serving traffic. That's why naive modulo sharding is a trap you only discover on the day you need to grow, which is the worst possible day to discover it.

exercises.prompt: What does consistent hashing fix about that?
choices: Adding or removing a node only remaps the keys near it, so roughly 1/n of the data moves instead of nearly all of it
It removes the need for a shard key
exercises.why: Keys and nodes are placed on the same ring, and each key belongs to the next node clockwise — so adding a node only steals the arc between it and its predecessor, leaving every other key exactly where it was. It makes growth incremental rather than catastrophic, which is the entire point. Note what it doesn't fix: a celebrity key is still one key, and the ring will happily hand it to one node.

exercises.prompt: Consistent hashing with few nodes distributes data unevenly. What's the standard fix?
choices: Virtual nodes — place each machine at many points on the ring, so the averaging smooths out the arcs
exercises.why: With three machines you get three arcs, and arcs land wherever the hash puts them — so one machine can easily own twice its share. Giving each machine hundreds of positions on the ring means it owns hundreds of small arcs whose sizes average out, and it also means a departing machine's load is inherited by many peers rather than dumped entirely on its one neighbour.

exercises.prompt: How does an application know which shard to talk to?
choices: It computes the rule itself, or asks a routing layer or directory that knows the current mapping
exercises.why: Either every client embeds the rule — fast, but now the mapping is duplicated in every deploy and changing it means coordinating a fleet — or a routing tier owns it, which costs a hop and becomes something that must itself be replicated. A directory adds flexibility, letting you move individual shards without redeploying clients, at the price of one more component in the request path that must never be wrong.

exercises.prompt: You need to move a shard's data to new machines while staying online. Slide toward your approach.
exercises.why: A big-bang move is short but has no safe abort: if the copy is wrong you discover it with live traffic on the new machines and no clean way back. The incremental path — write to both, backfill history, verify they agree, then shift reads — is longer and lets you stop at any step with the old shard still authoritative. When the thing you're moving is the source of truth, reversibility is worth far more than speed.

exercises.prompt: Your users are sharded across 16 machines. You run: 'count all users who signed up today.' What happens?
choices: All 16 are queried and the results combined — a scatter-gather, as slow as the slowest shard
exercises.why: The data for that question is spread across every machine, so the query has to visit all of them and merge — and it can't finish until the slowest one replies. That's unit 4's tail-latency problem arriving through your shard count: with 16 shards you draw 16 samples from the latency distribution every time, so the typical query now waits on roughly your p96 shard, and about one query in seven waits on a p99 one. Push the fan-out to 100 and the majority of queries wait on a p99 — the effect scales with how many shards you touch, which is another reason to keep queries on one.

exercises.prompt: You need to transfer money between two users who live on different shards, atomically. How hard is that?
choices: Easy — wrap it in a transaction
Hard: a normal transaction covers one database, so spanning shards needs distributed coordination — two-phase commit or a saga
exercises.why: Unit 9's boundary is exactly the shard: `BEGIN/COMMIT` protects one machine's data and knows nothing about the other shard, so atomicity across them needs the machinery you hoped to avoid — a coordinator that can block, or compensating actions and eventual consistency. This is why people shard so that transactions stay within a shard: put things that change together on the same machine, and the hard problem never arises.

exercises.prompt: Which get harder once you shard? Select all.
choices: Joins between tables on different shards
Looking up a single row by shard key
exercises.why: Anything requiring data from more than one machine becomes coordination — fan out and merge, or a distributed protocol. The single-key lookup is the one that stays easy, and in fact gets faster, since each shard is smaller. That asymmetry is the whole design principle: sharding rewards you for asking questions that live on one machine, and punishes every question that doesn't.

exercises.prompt: A year in, you realize you sharded by the wrong key. How bad is that?
choices: Severe: the key determined where every row physically lives, so changing it means relocating the entire dataset while serving traffic
exercises.why: The shard key isn't a setting, it's the physical layout of your data — so changing it is a full migration of everything, live, with application code that assumes the old key threaded throughout. This is why the choice deserves real thought before you make it: sharding is a one-way door, and the key is the hinge.

exercises.prompt: Your app is read-heavy, fits comfortably on one machine, but reads are overwhelming it. Should you shard?
choices: Yes — sharding is how you scale
No — the data fits and writes are fine, so caching and read replicas solve this without any of sharding's costs
Only if you have more than a million users
exercises.why: Sharding addresses write throughput and data size, and you have neither problem — so you'd take on cross-shard queries, distributed transactions, and a permanent key decision to fix something a cache handles for free. Match the tool to the actual bottleneck: reads want caching and replicas, writes and size want sharding.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of sharding?
choices: It's how real systems scale, so do it early
It's the only way past one machine's write and storage limits — and it costs you cross-shard queries, cross-shard transactions, and a key you can't easily change
It's obsolete now that machines are large
exercises.why: It's the last tool you reach for, because it's the only one that solves the write and size ceilings — and the only one whose costs are permanent and structural rather than tunable. Everything hard in this unit traced back to one fact: your data no longer lives in one place, so every question spanning it becomes coordination, which is precisely what unit 11 warned you that scaling out buys.
